response.translation: [343] GALEN, WHOM ONE MUST PURGE, AND WITH WHAT CATHARTICS, AND WHEN. Those who have healthy bodies are troublesome to purge; for they become dizzy and suffer griping, and the purgation proceeds with difficulty in them, and in addition to this they are, moreover, quickly exhausted. All these things come about because the cathartic drug strives to draw the humour proper to it, and, being at a loss for it, melts down the blood and the flesh, in order that it may draw from these what is proper to it.

For some, then, it is beneficial that the phlegmatic humours be evacuated, for others the bitter-bilious, for others the melancholic, for others the serous residue, according to the nature of the affections that habitually occur in them. For instance, a certain man is seized by melancholy every year if he is not purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn. But if they neglect these things, the purgations turn out troublesome, sometimes accompanied by gripings and certain vertigos, much nausea and bad pulse, faintness and distress. raw_text: {"translation": "For we know that this [heat], so far as depends on itself, is [351] harmed; rather, it is for the sake of the humours that produce it. It is necessary, therefore, that the benefit arising from the evacuation of the troublesome humours be greater than the harm which the body must of necessity suffer from the cathartic drugs. And the benefit is greater if the harmful humour is evacuated both without distress and in its entirety. In order for this to come about, one must first consider carefully whether the patient is suitably disposed for such a purgation. For those who are in a state resulting from many indigestions or from viscous or thick foods, and likewise those whose hypochondria are tense and distended with wind, or are excessively hot and fiery, or in whom there is also some inflammation of the viscera in that region—all these are unsuitable for purgations. It is necessary, therefore, that these conditions be absent, and that the patient's humours be as free-flowing as possible, that is, thin and partaking less of any viscosity, and that the passages through which the purgation is going to take place be opened wide. response.translation: But in acute diseases, right at the beginning—that is, on the first day, or not beyond the second—when we are going to employ [352] purgations at the time the humour is in turgor (ὀργᾷ), such a preparation cannot be carried out, unless perhaps one should have the opportunity to have unmixed melikraton made and given, having boiled in it some hyssop, or thyme, or origanum, or goat's-origanum, or pennyroyal, or some other of the things that thin in this way; so that with good reason we shall seldom have need of drugs at the beginning in acute diseases, because neither are the offending humours often in turgor at the beginning, nor, even if this is the case, would the patient be suited to the purgation, nor indeed does he afford us a suitable opportunity to prepare him. The humours are said to be in turgor when, having come into a more violent motion and flowing across from parts to parts, at the beginning of the disease they trouble the person, causing pain and nausea and tickling irritation and not permitting him to be at rest. But those already fixed in some one part one must neither set in motion by any other remedy nor purge with drugs before they have been concocted.
